prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of GLP-1 as an incretin hormone and of its physiological actions, which enabled incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six of us placed B042 first, but unanimity is not the argument. The argument is that this is one of the few cases where a specific physiological discovery (GLP-1 as an incretin and satiety signal, derived from proglucagon, with the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide identified and its insulinotropic action shown in humans) produced a discernible, large change in a field. Mature evidence supports it: independent confirmation over decades, multiple approved agents, and large randomized outcome trials showing cardiovascular and renal benefit. Holst on physiology, Mojsov on identification and synthesis of the active peptide, and Drucker on GLP-1/GLP-2 biology and receptor pharmacology cover the discovery chain within three names. Recognition is timely and arguably overdue.
statement.case_against: The credit problem is real. Habener and others made early peptide contributions and are not in the credited names, Mojsov's role is described differently in different accounts, and Knudsen's role in making durable, long-acting agonists is what actually reached patients. A prize that honours the biology but omits the drug developer can be read as incomplete, while one that includes Knudsen forces out a discoverer. I have not independently verified the priority details, and the three-person cap means someone with a strong claim will be left out whichever configuration we choose.

responses.point: B042 should include Knudsen alongside Drucker and Holst, since the arc from physiological discovery to long-acting analogues is what makes the story complete, with Mojsov as a difficult exclusion.
responses.response: I see the force of the complete-arc argument, but I disagree on the allocation. The prize recognises a discovery, and Mojsov's identification of the active peptide form is part of the discovery chain, whereas liraglutide and semaglutide are engineering of a known mechanism. The drug-development story is carried by the citation language (enabled treatment) rather than by a laureate slot. I would reconsider if the committee concludes Mojsov's priority cannot be defended, in which case Knudsen is the natural third name.

responses.point: The three most defensible B042 names are Holst, Drucker and Mojsov, with Knudsen as a major drug-development figure but not a discoverer; Linnarsson also ranked TOR (B006) second, leaving out Sabatini because of conduct questions.
responses.response: I agree on the B042 trio. On B006 I am less persuaded: leaving Sabatini out on unverified conduct concerns would be a judgment about a person that we should not make from recollection. The scientific question is separate: Hall's yeast genetics and the mammalian mTOR work are both essential, Schreiber's FKBP12-rapamycin chemistry is decisive too, and there is no clean three-person split. That unresolved allocation is why I rank B006 below B033 and B045.

responses.point: Svenningsson placed CAR-T (B049) second and the antisense SMN2 therapy (B027) third, valuing clear concept-to-therapy paths with dramatic clinical benefit.
responses.response: I take the clinical-benefit point seriously, and nusinersen is a striking example of mechanism-guided therapy. But B027 gained only partial support across the committee, and I am concerned that the Krainer and Bennett split between discovery and chemistry leaves it as a platform story still maturing. For CAR-T I would agree the clinical effect is proven, but credit remains the problem: Eshhar's original chimeric receptor is outside the credited list, so I am not comfortable making B049 my lead alternative.

responses.point: Sandberg proposed a two-person CAR-T configuration (June, Sadelain) as the cleanest, and ranked the unfolded protein response (B033) second as a clean Mori-Walter pair.
responses.response: I agree that B033 is the cleanest credit among the shortlist and I rank it as my first alternative for that reason. I disagree that dropping Rosenberg makes CAR-T clean: removing him narrows the adoptive-cell-therapy lineage while Eshhar still remains unaddressed, so two names do not repair the attribution problem, they only move it. The UPR has a stronger fundamental mechanism claim, though I accept the disease-level impact is still developing.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranked B033 second and B049 third, treating the UPR as a conceptually clean basic-science discovery whose therapeutic payoff is still emerging.
responses.response: I share the view that a basic-science prize does not need a finished therapy, and the UPR meets that bar. Where I differ is on priorities: with a single-achievement GLP-1 prize available and robustly supported, I would use the second slot only if the committee wants a two-part configuration, in which case Mori and Walter would be my preference. That would require trimming B042 to two names to stay within three people, which I do not think is worth the cost to attribution.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's contribution to identification of the active GLP-1 peptide is accepted as a decisive discovery credit, and how Habener's early contributions should be weighed.
Whether the committee prefers to place drug development (Knudsen) within a physiology prize or leave it to the citation.
Whether a two-part prize with B033 or B045 is worth the loss of a name from B042 under the three-person limit.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B042, B033, B045, B049, B006, B027 or B019. B012 (deep brain stimulation for Parkinson's disease) is close to my own Parkinson's-related research field, and I have documented co-authorship with Per Svenningsson, though neither bears on the configuration I propose.
